title: Origin, Corporate Evolution & Operating Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: How the Business Got Here — Pivots & Cycles
question: How did a 1960 Kolkata carbon black maker become a ₹8,189 crore, debt-carrying, three-platform chemicals group, and what did each boom and bust on the way teach about what this business earns through a cycle?

epigraph.quote: “We have to shift platforms from Carbon Black.”
epigraph.author: Dr Sanjiv Goenka, Chairman, PCBL conference call announcing the Aquapharm acquisition, 28 November 2023

web_blocks.html: PCBL Chemical Limited is a 1960 carbon black maker. In FY2026 it reports ₹8,189 crore of revenue across three platforms: rubber and specialty blacks (the carbon black segment, 79.5% of revenue), Aquapharm’s specialty chemicals (17.6%) and a pre-revenue battery-materials venture. Captive power sits underneath, at 2.9% of revenue but 24% of segment profit [3]. The history matters to an owner because it explains three things the later chapters keep returning to. The carbon black engine has grown by buying or building capacity and then filling it for sixty years. Its profit swings with feedstock and spreads far more than its revenue does. Its balance sheet also changed character on 31 January 2024, when a debt-funded acquisition ended nine years (FY2015–FY2023) in which year-end borrowings stayed between ₹617 crore and ₹1,220 crore [4].

The company was incorporated on 31 March 1960 “in collaboration with Phillips Petroleum Company, USA”. The Integrated Report adds that it “was established in 1960 under the leadership of Mr. K. P. Goenka” [3][17]. Production began on 5 June 1962 at Durgapur, West Bengal, with 14,000 MTPA of oil-furnace carbon black [17][47]. A technical collaboration with Columbian Chemicals (USA) followed in 1988, together with a 4 MW co-generation unit that burned the process tail gas for power [17]. Organic growth was slow: Durgapur took 33 years to reach 78,000 MTPA. The pace changed with acquisitions and new sites. Palej (Gujarat) was bought from Gujarat Carbon in November 1996, adding 25,000 MTPA. Kochi (Kerala) came through the amalgamation of Carbon & Chemicals India, with company sources giving 1996, 1997 and 1998 for the year [17][19][47]. The port-side Mundra greenfield started in October 2009 with 90,000 MTPA and a 16 MW power plant, while Durgapur’s power plant went from 4 MW to 30 MW [17][47]. By 2013 the company’s own chart shows 472,000 MTPA, 6.1 times the 1995 level [19].

web_blocks.takeaway: Capacity grew 6.1 times from 1995 to 2013 and only 1.28 times from 2013 to 2021, the debottlenecking years. It then grew 46% in the five years from 603,000 (2021) to 880,000 (FY2026), a 7.9% annual rate [19][3]. For 2024 the company gives no explanation of one step. We infer that the 20,000 MTPA Mundra specialty line of July 2023 is the unlisted balance of the +104,000 step. The 1 million MTPA target for FY2028 depends on a greenfield plant that has not started (Chapter 5) [3].

web_blocks.html: Nameplate flatters, and the placement document shows by how much. Effective capacity (adjusted for product mix) was 81–84% of installed in FY2019–FY2021. FY2019 production of 410,798 t was 92.4% of effective capacity but 77.7% of installed; FY2020 was 86.6% and 71.5%; FY2021 was 82.3% and 66.9% [47]. FY2026 production was 619,458 t (495,563 t standalone plus 123,895 t at the Tamil Nadu subsidiary) [3]. That is 78.4% of the 790,000 MTPA opening capacity or 70.4% of the 880,000 MTPA year-end figure (our arithmetic). Standalone production was flat on FY2025’s 496,944 t, so Tamil Nadu carried all the growth [3]. Co-generation capacity rose from 76 MW (FY2018–FY2021) to 84, 98, 110 and 122 MW in FY2022–FY2025. Another 12 MW is under construction in Tamil Nadu [20][18].

web_blocks.takeaway: Three points correct what circulates in summaries. There was no name change in 2018; 2018 was the 1:5 sub-division and fund-raising approval [73]. The first rename sits around the turn of 2021–22. The October 2021 placement document still carries the old name, and the 9 February 2022 filing already signs as PCBL Limited [47][49]. The Tamil Nadu brownfield was also two tranches, not a single 30,000 MTPA addition: a 60,000 MTPA line from 28 January 2026 and then 30,000 MTPA from 27 March 2026 [3].

web_blocks.html: The share record has few, large actions. The 2021 placement had no named project (general corporate purposes, capex, debt repayment and working capital) [47]. It lifted the pre-split share count to 18,87,31,302. That is why the feed’s equity capital rises from ₹34 crore in FY2021 to ₹38 crore in FY2022 (our arithmetic; the feed gives no cause) [47][4]. After the 2022 split, with record date 12 April 2022, the count stayed at 37,74,62,604. The warrant conversion of 3 November 2025 then added 1.6 crore shares (+4.24%) [50][3]. The Integrated Report records no buyback and no bonus issue in the last five years [3].

web_blocks.title: Twelve years of cycles in one table

web_blocks.caption: Operating cycle, FY2015–FY2026, trailing twelve months to September 2026 and H1 FY27; ₹ crore unless stated; consolidated
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: the price-blind Screener feed [4], with H1 FY27 revenue, PAT and cash flow from the company’s Q2 FY27 update [18]. Margins and growth are computed from the feed. Operating profit here excludes other income, so it runs below the company’s own EBITDA. The company figure adds other income back (FY2026: ₹1,082 crore company versus ₹1,043 crore feed; Q2 FY27: ₹310 crore versus ₹294 crore) [18]. For FY2023 the Q4 FY24 deck shows revenue of ₹5,874 crore, while ICRA, the feed and the FY2023 base elsewhere show ₹5,774 crore. We use ₹5,774 crore [5][42]. n/p means not published.

web_blocks.html: Revenue grew 3.3 times in eleven years (11.5% a year), operating profit 6.9 times and PAT 20 times, though the last starts from a trivial ₹10 crore. The comparison that tells the story is FY2019 to FY2026. Revenue rose 2.3 times and operating profit 1.7 times, yet PAT fell to 0.52 times its FY2019 level (₹383 crore to ₹198 crore). PAT margin fell from 10.9% to 2.4% and ROCE from 25% to 8%. Capital employed (equity plus borrowings including leases) grew 3.7 times, from ₹2,442 crore to ₹8,995 crore [4]. Scale was added faster than earnings, and interest absorbed 41% of FY2026 operating profit against 6% in FY2019 (our arithmetic).

web_blocks.title: Boom and bust, cycle by cycle

web_blocks.html: FY2015–FY2016, the reset. Revenue fell 23% to ₹1,894 crore while operating margin rose from 6.1% to 8.7%. Borrowings fell from ₹1,220 crore to ₹1,022 crore, and cash from operations was ₹422 crore against operating profit of ₹165 crore [4]. We found no primary document explaining FY2016. Falling revenue with a rising margin and a large working-capital release is what a formula-priced business shows when input prices fall. The reason is that lower pass-through prices cut revenue while the spread per tonne holds [24]; that is our inference. The feed also shows reserves more than doubling (₹473 crore to ₹1,010 crore) on a PAT of ₹16 crore, a restatement we could not source. At ₹1,900 crore of sales the business still earned almost nothing for owners, because interest (₹72 crore) and depreciation (₹62 crore) took most of the ₹165 crore operating profit.

FY2017–FY2019, the boom. Operating profit rose from ₹265 crore to ₹616 crore, margin from 13.8% to 17.5%, PAT from ₹69 crore to ₹383 crore and ROCE from 11% to 25% [4]. Plants ran at 92.4% of effective capacity in FY2019, and the anti-dumping duty on Chinese and Russian imports was in force [47][55]. A January 2018 press report records third-quarter profit up almost four-fold to ₹57 crore, “riding on the back of higher sales and better capacity utilisation” [73]. Borrowings stayed between ₹717 crore and ₹793 crore and interest fell to ₹37 crore, so almost all of the gain reached owners. The lesson is that the business earns its best returns when plants are full and imports are fenced. Neither is in management’s hands.

FY2020–FY2021, Covid. Revenue fell 8% in FY2020 and 18% in FY2021 to ₹2,660 crore. Carbon black volume fell only 4.3% to 389,261 t because the damage was confined to the first-quarter lockdown [47]. Operating margin reached 19.4%, the highest of the twelve years, because materials cost fell to 60.5% of revenue from 67.5% on cheaper feedstock [47]. PAT was ₹314 crore in a year when revenue was down 18%. Revenue is the wrong dial here. Feedstock cost and spread per tonne moved profit, and a cheap-feedstock year beat several full-volume years.

FY2022–FY2023, the feedstock spike. Revenue rose 67% to ₹4,446 crore and 30% to ₹5,774 crore, largely on price (FY2023 volume was 445,184 t). Operating margin slid from 19.4% to 14.7% and 12.7% [4][24]. Company EBITDA per tonne still rose to ₹17,405 in FY2023 [24]. Managing Director Kaushik Roy explained on 15 May 2023: “The raw material price increase, we are kind of immune to cost increase or decrease because in most cases, we have a formula understanding with our customers. So, whether it increases or it decreases, it is normally a pass-through for us.” [24]. Pass-through protects rupees per tonne, not margin percentages, and it inflates working capital. Free cash flow on the feed’s measure was negative in both years (–₹16 crore and –₹392 crore) while the ₹400 crore placement and the Chennai greenfield absorbed cash [4][47].

FY2024, the acquisition year. Revenue rose 11% to ₹6,420 crore, operating margin was 16.2% and PAT ₹491 crore, the highest of the twelve years. That year held only two months of Aquapharm (₹239 crore of revenue and ₹22.8 crore of PBT) [2]. Borrowings went from ₹1,029 crore to ₹4,983 crore and total assets doubled to ₹11,295 crore. Quarterly interest jumped from ₹33 crore in Q3 to ₹108 crore in Q4 [4]. The year looks fine because the cost arrives later; the first real test of the deal was FY2025.

FY2025, the peak on borrowed money. Revenue rose 31% to ₹8,404 crore, with Aquapharm in for a full year (₹1,420 crore) and carbon black volume at 596,262 t (+12%, exports +22%) [9][3]. Mr Roy told the 29 April 2025 call that PCBL Chemical “has reported its best ever operational performance and highest ever EBITDA” [32]. Company EBITDA was a record ₹1,384 crore. Interest of ₹461 crore and depreciation of ₹346 crore took PAT down from ₹491 crore to ₹435 crore. Cash from operations of ₹760 crore did not cover capex of ₹774 crore [4][3]. A ₹554.72 crore goodwill impairment on Aquapharm was offset by a ₹554.20 crore deferred-tax reversal after the December 2024 merger [2]. The two items left profit almost untouched. At an 8% cost of debt and a larger depreciation base, record EBITDA is not record profit.

FY2026, the trough. Revenue fell 3% to ₹8,189 crore on record volume of 618,956 t (+4%). EBITDA per tonne fell 25% to ₹14,939 from ₹19,930, company EBITDA to ₹1,082 crore (–22%) and PAT to ₹198 crore (–54%) [14][3]. Q3 PAT was ₹2 crore after a ₹21 crore labour-code exceptional charge that carried no tax credit in the quarter. That produced an 80% quarterly tax rate that the company did not explain (the tax reading is ours) [4]. Management named softer global spreads, surplus domestic capacity, US tariffs, the West Asia conflict from February 2026, the quarter-lag in formula pricing and weak Aquapharm oil and gas demand [3][37]. ICRA revised its outlook to Negative on 12 February 2026 and cited “subdued carbon black realisations across both the domestic and international markets due to supply overhang and increased dumping”. CARE followed on 7 July 2026 [44][46]. A record year for tonnes produced the lowest PAT since FY2017.

H1 FY27, a recovery that needs caveats. Revenue was ₹4,948 crore (+16%), company EBITDA ₹710 crore (+18%) and PAT ₹229 crore (+47%). Volume was 8.9% lower (287,694 t against 315,821 t), with Q2 volume down 17% [18]. The CFO calls the volume loss “primarily a margin decision” to drop low-margin spot and South-East Asian orders [40]. Two items flatter the half: about ₹70 crore of inventory gains in Q1 and a ₹33 crore US tariff refund in Q2 [39][40]. Stripping both, we estimate H1 EBITDA at about ₹607 crore against ₹603 crore a year earlier. That is flat, not +18% (our arithmetic). The lesson, still provisional, is that price and one-offs can lift a half with no improvement in volume or mix.

web_blocks.takeaway: Across five different cycles one lever, spread per tonne, explained profit, and revenue explained almost nothing. FY2024 interest of 3.4 times compares ₹181 crore with FY2023’s ₹53 crore [4]. Chapter 3 turns spread into per-tonne unit economics. Chapter 6 audits the cash behind these profits.

web_blocks.title: The Aquapharm acquisition: the pivot that changed the balance sheet

web_blocks.html: Aquapharm Chemicals Pvt Ltd is a Pune company founded in 1974. It is among the world’s top phosphonate producers, with plants at Mahad and Pirangut (Maharashtra), Texas and Jeddah. ICRA names Procter & Gamble, Henkel, Ecolab and Unilever on its client list [3][21][42]. PCBL signed the share purchase agreement on 28 November 2023 for an aggregate ₹3,851.49 crore (the headline was ₹3,800 crore) for 100% of the company. It closed on 31 January 2024, with a net cash outflow of ₹3,707.97 crore after ₹103 crore of acquired cash [2]. The Chairman said the sellers, a joint venture between two families, wanted to cash out and that three parties bid [27]. The deal was “financed through a mix of internal accruals and external funds”. The group raised ₹2,500 crore externally, including ₹700 crore of NCDs by PCBL and ₹550 crore by the acquisition vehicle, Advaya Chemical Industries [2]. ICRA’s verdict was that it was “majorly funded through external debt” [44]. Chapter 6 holds the forensic detail on goodwill, the purchase-price allocation and the debt. The question here is how the deal case compares with what followed.

web_blocks.takeaway: The Chairman’s forecast was struck on FY2023 numbers. The pro forma disclosure shows the revenue base had already slipped by about a quarter before the deal closed (₹1,553 crore against ₹2,045 crore described). Two sources disagree on capacity (167,000 versus 256,747 MTPA), and we cannot reconcile them. At the group’s 7.8% average cost of debt, the ₹2,500 crore of external funds alone costs about ₹195 crore a year (our arithmetic). That is more than Aquapharm’s FY2026 EBITDA of ₹162 crore.

web_blocks.html: The fair reading has two sides. The bull case is that Aquapharm gave PCBL a global specialty platform with 275+ products and 265+ customers on three continents. The bull case also holds that H1 FY27 EBITDA of ₹89 crore was up 47%, that integration has helped procurement, and that a provisional anti-dumping duty on two phosphonates from China may help [3][18]. The bear case is that an unrelated chemistry was bought near the top of its cycle and that EBITDA reached only 45% of the FY2025 forecast and 31% of the FY2026 forecast. Guidance has also drifted: “20–25%” growth and a ₹75 crore quarterly run-rate in April 2026 became “double-digit” growth in November 2026, against actual quarters of ₹29 crore, ₹47 crore and ₹42 crore. Aquapharm’s chief executive also changed in 2026 [37][40][35]. On the record to date the bear evidence is stronger. The bull case rests on a recovery not yet visible in margins.

web_blocks.title: The other pivots: Tamil Nadu, specialty lines, US and Saudi plants, batteries

web_blocks.html: Tamil Nadu. The Chennai greenfield (PCBL (TN) Ltd) started in September 2023 with 63,000 MTPA. It reached 147,000 MTPA on three lines in 2024 at about ₹950 crore including 24 MW of power, and made ₹35.99 crore of PAT in FY2026 (₹10.69 crore in FY2025) [42][17][3]. The brownfield addition was slower. Management said in January 2025 that the first 30,000 MTPA phase was weeks away, and repeated it in April and July 2025. Commercial production came on 27 March 2026, with the 60,000 MTPA Line 4 from 28 January 2026 [31][32][33][3]. Specialty black. Three 20,000 MTPA lines at Mundra (July 2023, December 2024, Q1 FY27) took specialty nameplate to 132,000 MTPA [17][42]. The MD said on 2 November 2026, though, that “the capacity that we have is around 75” because specialty feedstock is the constraint [40]. US and Saudi plants. These came with Aquapharm (Texas via APChem, acquired in 2017 and producing from 2019, and Jeddah via USCI, acquired in 2019) [21]. PCBL’s own overseas build is an innovation centre in Belgium (2020), PCBL Chemical USA Inc. (formed 23 July 2025) and a warehouse in Antwerp [3][18]. Batteries. The Chairman said on 28 November 2023 that “the next phase is going to be chemicals, which go into electric vehicles” [27]. The Nanovace JV followed in March 2024, with ₹194.80 crore and ₹33.52 crore invested in FY2025 and FY2026. The pilot plant, promised “in the next few months” in April 2025, was “creating some samples” on 2 November 2026 [3][32][40]. A 1,000 MTPA super-conductive carbon line at Palej is operational, and an acetylene-black technology transfer was signed with Ningxia Jinhua. Separately, 116.62 acres at Naidupeta, Andhra Pradesh, are held for a 300,000 MTPA plant, and CARE puts its first 150,000 MTPA phase at about ₹1,100 crore [17][3][46].

web_blocks.title: Who has run it: promoters, board and management

web_blocks.html: Dr Sanjiv Goenka has been on the board since 30 October 1986 and chairs it; Shashwat and Preeti Goenka are non-executive directors [3][47]. Rainbow Investments Ltd is classed as the parent “under de facto control” and held 47.43% after the 2025 conversion. The promoter group held 53.37%, up from 51.40% [3]. The 2021 placement document shows the promoter group at 53.56% of the pre-issue capital (9,23,07,785 shares), falling to 48.91% after the issue [47]. It was 51.41% by December 2023 and held 19,40,36,210 shares after the split [3][4]. That is about 0.94 crore more than the pre-issue holding on a post-split basis, so the group added shares in between, though our sources do not say when or how. The ₹448 crore of promoter warrants (₹112 crore paid in FY2025, ₹336 crore in FY2026) is the only promoter equity infusion in the period [3]. Chapter 6 covers how much came back as dividends.

Executive leadership turned over at the top while the finance chief stayed. Kaushik Roy, a director since 5 February 2013 and Managing Director from 5 February 2019, led the company through the whole Aquapharm deal, the FY2025 peak and the FY2026 trough. He resigned on 3 November 2025 “due to personal reasons”, 17 days after leading the Q2 FY26 call [3][47]. His successor Nilesh Koul (five-year term, approved by postal ballot on 11 December 2025) came from Hindalco, where he led aluminium downstream. His background is in metals, oil and gas and FMCG rather than carbon black [81][3]. Rohit Narang is the chief executive of Aquapharm only, not of the group. He joined in May 2026 after Suresh Kalra’s resignation was disclosed on 3 February 2026 [82][35]. Raj Kumar Gupta has been CFO on every call read from July 2022 [22]. Rituraj Singh Kalra joins as Executive Director for International Markets (rubber blacks) on 9 November 2026 [86]. Paras K. Chowdhary, an independent director since 24 December 1999, also sat on the boards of RPG Enterprises and CEAT Kelani Holdings. He completed his final term on 21 July 2024 [47][3].

web_blocks.title: What the history means for an owner
paragraphs: PCBL has rebuilt itself three times. The first rebuild took it from one Durgapur plant to a national network by 2013. The second made a five-plant maker with specialty lines out of a four-plant commodity producer by 2024. The third turned a carbon black pure-play into a three-platform group in 2024. Each rebuild added capacity or a business faster than it added earnings. The FY2019 to FY2026 record (revenue 2.3 times, PAT 0.52 times) is the arithmetic result.

The plants have arrived late but arrived. The promises that depended on a new business or on balance-sheet repair (Aquapharm’s forecasts, the 30-month debt payback, the battery pilot) have slipped or been missed. An owner should value the carbon black engine on mid-cycle spreads. Aquapharm is an asset still earning below its cost of debt, and batteries are an option with no revenue yet. Chapter 2 now looks at what each segment makes, sells and earns.

web_blocks.html: What would change our mind: two consecutive years in which Aquapharm’s EBITDA exceeds ₹250 crore (the low end of the CFO’s May 2024 guide) and carbon black EBITDA per tonne holds above ₹17,000 with volume growth. Together these would show the FY2024 pivot earning its cost of capital. Another missed Aquapharm guide would push our view the other way.

book_paragraphs: Come with me to the gate of the Durgapur plant on 5 June 1962. A company incorporated two years earlier, in collaboration with Phillips Petroleum of the United States, lights a furnace that will turn carbon-rich oil into 14,000 tonnes a year of fine black powder. Inside the reactor, at 1,400 to 1,900 degrees Celsius, the oil cracks in a few milliseconds; a water spray stops the reaction; bag filters separate the powder from the gas; and the powder is pelletised with a molasses solution. The leftover gas, which has a calorific value of about 650 to 700 kilocalories, is burned for steam and power. That powder is what makes a tyre black and, more importantly, what lets rubber survive tens of thousands of kilometres. You and I will spend several chapters on it, so fix one idea now: this company’s whole story is capacity, how it is built, bought and filled, and a cycle, the way the spread between feedstock cost and selling price swings the profit.

Look at how the capacity arrived. Durgapur needed 33 years to reach 78,000 tonnes. Then, between 1996 and 1998, the company bought Palej from Gujarat Carbon and absorbed Kochi, and by 2013 its own chart shows 472,000 tonnes, six times the 1995 level. The port-side Mundra plant of October 2009 was the bold greenfield step. A long plateau followed, only 1.28 times between 2013 and 2021, and then a new burst from 603,000 tonnes in 2021 to 880,000 in FY2026. Here is something an analyst learns to check: what the nameplate hides. In FY2019, the boom year, the plants ran at 92.4 percent of what the company calls effective capacity, yet only 77.7 percent of installed. If someone quotes you a utilisation number, always ask which denominator they are using.

Now let us walk through the money cycle between 2015 and 2021, because it teaches the most for the least cost. In FY2016 revenue fell 23 percent, yet margin rose and cash flow from operations was ₹422 crore on an operating profit of only ₹165 crore. I could not find a company document that explains that year, so I will say only what the pattern suggests: a formula-priced business whose input prices fell. Then the boom, FY2017 to FY2019: operating profit up from ₹265 crore to ₹616 crore, return on capital employed from 11 to 25 percent, plants nearly full, anti-dumping duty still shielding the market. A press report in January 2018 caught the mood, quoting third-quarter profit almost four times higher “riding on the back of higher sales and better capacity utilisation”. That duty lapsed at the end of 2020, when the Finance Ministry declined to extend it, so every cycle since has been fought without that fence.

Covid is the year that should change how you read this company. In FY2021 revenue fell 18 percent, and operating margin hit 19.4 percent, the best of twelve years. How? Cheaper feedstock took materials from 67.5 percent of revenue to 60.5. Volume had barely moved, down 4.3 percent. So which number would you have been staring at, revenue or spread? Then came FY2022 and FY2023, when revenue rose 67 and then 30 percent. The Managing Director, Kaushik Roy, put the mechanism plainly on 15 May 2023: “The raw material price increase, we are kind of immune to cost increase or decrease because in most cases, we have a formula understanding with our customers.” Notice what he did not say. Immune in rupees per tonne, yes; immune in margin percentage, no, because revenue swelled while the spread did not, and working capital swallowed the cash. Free cash flow was negative in both years while the Chennai greenfield went up.

Between the Covid year and the Aquapharm deal there is a quieter story you should not skip, because it shows how this company behaves when it builds. In October 2021 it raised ₹400 crore from institutions without naming a project. In 2023 the Chennai greenfield began producing: 63,000 tonnes in phase one, 147,000 tonnes on three lines by 2024, for about ₹950 crore including its own power plant. Mr Roy was candid about the ramp on 15 May 2023: Chennai would run at roughly 40 to 50 percent of capacity that year, and “It honestly depends on the approval process of different customers and the time required for that.” That sentence is the moat and the weakness in one. A tyre maker must approve each grade from each plant before it buys, which slows any rival, and it also means that new capacity does not fill by itself. By FY2026 the Chennai subsidiary earned ₹36 crore of profit after tax, about 3.8 percent of what the plant cost. Capacity is built quickly; returns arrive slowly.

On 28 November 2023 the Chairman, Dr Sanjiv Goenka, called the market within an hour of signing a share purchase agreement for Aquapharm, a Pune-based phosphonate maker, at ₹3,851 crore. He said the sellers, a joint venture between two families, wanted to cash out, that three parties had bid, and that PCBL had been clear it would not go above its number. He said both companies were debt free, that PCBL would borrow first and that over 30 months the combined cash flow would repay it all. And then came the line I find most revealing about the man and the company: “I am personally very debt averse. I have said that time and time again. I’m uncomfortable when we have debt. I frankly don’t get sleep if we have debt.” Hold that sentence in your mind, because the next two years tested it.

An analyst on that call, Abhijeet Bora, asked the question every sceptic would ask: at nine to ten percent on borrowed money, would Aquapharm’s EBITDA simply “be absorbed by the interest itself”? The Chairman’s answer was that this was true for the first year, but “for the first full year that we have Aquapharm, we do believe that we will be bottom line and margin accretive.” Here is what then happened. In FY2024 only two months of Aquapharm were consolidated, so profit looked fine at ₹491 crore, while borrowings jumped from ₹1,029 crore to ₹4,983 crore and quarterly interest went from ₹33 crore to ₹108 crore. In FY2025 the first full year brought record EBITDA of ₹1,384 crore and, as Mr Roy told the call, the “best ever operational performance”, yet PAT fell to ₹435 crore because interest and depreciation had grown so much.

Do the arithmetic with me. The Chairman’s forecast for Aquapharm’s EBITDA was ₹380 crore, ₹430 crore and ₹525 crore for FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026. The CFO told investors on 23 May 2024 that Aquapharm “on a full year basis is going to add another 250 to 300 crore”. The actual numbers were ₹194 crore for FY2025 and ₹162 crore for FY2026, which is 45 percent and 31 percent of the forecast. Management itself said, on the 29 April 2025 call, that “FY '25 was a bit challenging year for Aquapharm”, blaming a yellow-phosphorus crisis. And there is a quieter clue in the FY2025 annual report: its pro forma disclosure implies that Aquapharm’s revenue for the twelve months to March 2024 was about ₹1,553 crore, a quarter below the ₹2,045 crore described on the call. The deal case was built on a number that had already slipped. I would not call that deception, because I see no evidence of it. I would call it the oldest mistake in acquisitions: pricing a business off its best recent year.

To be fair, weigh both sides. The bull case says PCBL bought a global specialty platform with more than 265 customers, the new chief executive talks sensibly about utilisation and mix, and H1 FY27 EBITDA of ₹89 crore was up 47 percent. The bear case says the margin fell from 13.7 to 11.2 percent, the guidance has been trimmed, the segment earned 0.4 percent pre-tax on its assets in FY2026, and the leadership changed within a year. An analyst put it bluntly on the 3 February 2026 call: “we have not been able to ramp up Aquapharm, like it has been a very long period of time now.” On the record to date I weigh the bear case heavier, and I put perhaps a one-in-four chance on Aquapharm reaching the old ₹250 crore EBITDA level within two years. You can put your own number on it, but put one.

FY2026 is where the threads meet. Record volume of 618,956 tonnes, and PAT down 54 percent to ₹198 crore. In the December quarter profit was ₹2 crore. Spread per tonne had fallen from ₹19,930 to ₹14,939, and that single number explains almost everything. Managing Director Nilesh Koul said on 30 April 2026: “Spread appear to have found a floor, exit quarter momentum has turned positive.” The first half of FY27 then brought profit up 47 percent on 9 percent lower volume, and I want you to hold the same suspicion you hold for any rebound: about ₹70 crore of inventory gains in the first quarter and a ₹33 crore tariff refund in the second. Take those out and my estimate is that half-year EBITDA of about ₹607 crore is flat on last year’s ₹603 crore. The CFO’s remark of 2 November 2026 carries the discipline: “We are not chasing volumes. We would rather keep this capacity spare.” That is a sound instinct for a price-taker, and it is also an admission about what the spot market is paying.

The balance sheet noticed. ICRA revised its outlook on PCBL’s AA rating to Negative on 12 February 2026, saying the pressure on profitability was “likely to persist over the next few quarters” and that the “continued weak performance” of Aquapharm would add to it; CARE made the same move on 7 July 2026. Neither agency questions liquidity, and no default or covenant breach is reported, though the annual report notes that deferment of financial covenants was obtained where needed. The point for a long-term owner is simple: the room for further error is thinner than it was in 2023, when the company said it was debt free.

One more pivot deserves a raised eyebrow: batteries. On 15 May 2023 Mr Roy said the battery-grade carbon was still in the laboratory: “I guess we will be there very soon.” By 28 November 2023 the Chairman told investors that the next phase would be “chemicals, which go into electric vehicles”. The Nanovace joint venture followed in March 2024, with ₹228 crore of convertible debentures invested over two years, and a pilot plant that was due “in the next few months” in April 2025, “within the coming weeks” in April 2026, and finally “started creating some samples” on 2 November 2026. The segment has no revenue and a loss of ₹0.15 crore. Does that mean batteries will fail? No. It means that three and a half years after “very soon” the company is at the sampling stage, while a leader such as Sila opened its first US factory in September 2025 after fourteen years of research. Treat batteries as an option, and price it at what you have already seen it cost: time and capital.

Finally, the people, because history is made by them. The business moved from its Phillips Petroleum origins to the RPSG Group, where Dr Goenka has sat on the board since 1986. Kaushik Roy ran it as Managing Director from February 2019 through the build-out, the Aquapharm deal and the peak, then resigned on 3 November 2025, 17 days after leading the Q2 FY26 call. Nilesh Koul came from Hindalco’s aluminium downstream business, so he is an operator without a carbon black background, which may be a strength or a gap. Note a correction that confuses many readers: Rohit Narang is the chief executive of Aquapharm only, from May 2026; the group is run by the Managing Director. The promoter group put in ₹448 crore through warrants and now holds 53.37 percent. The CFO, Raj Gupta, has been on every call for more than four years, which is the steadiest thing in this story.

So what do you carry from this chapter into the next? Three things. First, spread per tonne, not revenue, explains profit in every cycle since 2015. Second, the plants arrive late but arrive, while the promises tied to new businesses and to balance-sheet repair have slipped. Third, the company you are judging today is a group of three platforms with a ₹4,825 crore debt load, earning a pre-tax return on capital of about 8 percent against a cost of debt near 7.8 percent. Chapter 2 now opens each platform and asks what a customer would ask: who buys this, why, at what price, and how is it made?

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: I keep coming back to the pro forma number: about ₹1,553 crore of Aquapharm revenue for the year to March 2024 against ₹2,045 crore described at signing. A deal case is a promise about the future built on a photograph of the past, and this photograph was taken near the top of the cycle. The lesson is not that the buyer was foolish. It is that when a company pays for a cyclical business at its best recent earnings, using debt at a fixed cost, the margin for error is only as wide as the next downturn.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Notice how the company’s cleanest successes are the ones you can pour concrete for: Mundra, Chennai, the specialty lines. They arrive a few quarters late but they arrive. The promises that missed were about things that cannot be poured: a new business’s earnings, a debt schedule, a battery pilot. When you read management guidance, ask which kind of promise it is before you decide how much weight to give it.

book_callouts.title: Spread, not revenue
book_callouts.text: In a formula-priced commodity business, revenue is the sum of two things: a pass-through of feedstock cost and a margin per tonne. Only the second belongs to owners. When you read a cycle, convert revenue into spread per tonne first. In FY2026 revenue fell 3 percent while EBITDA per tonne fell 25 percent, and the second number was the real news.
